newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seven vie to be Seoul ruling party candidate.
newsitem.headline: Seven vie to be Seoul ruling party candidate.

text.p: South Korean ruling party presidential hopefuls, nicknamed the "seven dragons", on Wednesday formally kicked off a race to win the party's nomination.
A party spokesman said former party chairman Lee Hoi-chang and six others registered their candidacy before a deadline on Wednesday for a ticket in presidential elections in December.
The New Korea Party is due to elect its candidate in a national convention on July 21. Kim Young-sam, Korea's scandal-tainted president, cannot seek reelection under the constitution.

Political analysts and party officials said they expected stiff competition between Lee, Governor Rhee In-je of Kyonggi Province which surrounds Seoul, and former prime minister and legal scholar Lee Soo-sung.
Lee Hoi-chang, who stood down as party chairman on Tuesday, has been leading in most public polls among the seven due largely to his reputation as "Mr.Clean".
The former supreme court judge won his fame after he stood down as premier following a policy row with President Kim in 1993.
Kim appointed him as party chairman in March in a bid to restore the ruling camp's tarnished image following a string of scandals involving party members and the president's son.
A party faction loyal to Kim, however, indicated that it would campaign against Lee Hoi-chang in favour of either Governor Rhee or Lee Soo-sung, who have always toed Kim's line.
Kim has repeatedly said he would remain neutral, but political analysts say his supporters would work behind the scenes to install Kim's protege in office.

"Lee Hoi-chang has expanded his power base in the party using his post as chairman. He is now the front-runner but Kim loyalists, if united, will make his bid tough," said Choi Jang-jip, who lectures on politics at Korea University.

Kim Dae-jung, leader of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics, and Kim Jong-pil, head of the United Liberal Democrats, have already been nominated as opposition presidential candidates.
The two parties have been negotiating to field a single candidate to improve the opposition's chance in the December vote but their efforts so far have gone nowhere.
Kim Byung-kook, political science professor at Korea University, noted that no opposition party candidate had won in presidential elections in the past.
"Unless the New Korea Party falls apart and one of the hopefuls leaves the party to run separately, the ruling party candidate is likely to win," he said.

The other four ruling party "dragons" are President Kim's long-time aide Kim Deog-ryong, prosecutor-turned-lawmaker Lee Han-dong, former Seoul mayor Choe Byung-yul, and populist Park Chan-jong, who ran unsuccessfully for the presidency in 1992.
